You use the conditionals to talk about real or unreal possibilities in the present or future.
In speaking, you often use if with will, would, can or could to make a polite request:
If we can move on to the next item, we'll get through the list in no time.
If you could just wait there for a moment, I'll be right with you.
If you'll come this way, please.

images.text:
Candice: Amy! Just the person I was looking for. If you could follow me, please.
Amy: Right behind you.
Candice: So, did you hear the numbers from the auction?
Amy: Yeah, I guess you must be a little bit disappointed. I heard someone say $37,000. Not bad, but not exact--

Candice: If I can interject for a moment. We didn't raise $37,000, we actually exceeded our goal by $37,000. We raised $137,000 total!
Amy: Amazing, if I may say so myself! I guess I shouldn't be surprised, the turnout was really spectacular.
Candice: You ought to take some of the credit. Your speech really shed light on a very dire situation. You really did a good job of getting the audience to empathize with the children of Lesotho. If you don't mind, I'd like to use you as our official spokesperson.
Amy: Wow, it would be an honor.
Candice: You have got to take some time to celebrate. Why don't you take the afternoon off?
Amy: I ought to, but I can't. I really have to get these tax receipts out.

Candice: I don't think you have to do that for the small donations. It's really just for the larger amounts.
Amy: Actually, if you'll take a look at this. It says right there in the tax code: “A receipt shall be issued for any donation exceeding $10.”
Candice: It looks like you're on top of things, as always. I guess that's it, then.
Amy: If I could just add one more thing. I really am indebted to you for mentorship. You've really taught me a lot these past few weeks.
Candice: It's been a pleasure having you. In fact, I don't know what we ever did without you!
